summary:
Sleeping Beauties is an interactive storytelling platform which teaches space loving school age children about the equipment that humans have left on the Moon, Mars and in deep space. Each piece of equipment is turned into a bedtime story, using authentic NASA images, videos and audio as well as bespoke illustrations, lullabies and animations to tell how it works.

There are detailed summaries, timelines and 3D interactive models to help curious minds learn how each piece of equipment works. An interactive solar system along with maps of the Moon, Mars and deep space will also tell them exactly where each of the machines are now, what status they are currently in and what data they have gathered. There are also fun games and quizzes!

This platform solves the problem by providing a story driven learning experience. Children will learn how each piece of equipment works, and how the engineering links to the science they enabled, making them feel personally connected to these forgotten explorers.

This is important as children will often only be told about active missions. This gives the machines a voice and inspires future scientists and inventors.
details:
What Sleeping Beauties does

The challenge asks for the story of hardware NASA left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space, told to school-age space enthusiasts together with the science it made possible. Sleeping Beauties answers every part:

  • Hardware on the Moon: 15 machines on a 3D Moon globe at their real landing or impact sites (6 Apollo lunar modules, 5 Surveyors, 3 Rangers and Lunar Prospector), plus the 3 Apollo Moon buggies and the ALSEP science stations.
  • Hardware on Mars: 10 machines on a 3D Mars globe, from Viking 1 (1976) to Perseverance and the Ingenuity helicopter.
  • Hardware in deep space: 8 explorers in a 3D solar system: Voyager 1 and 2, Pioneer 10 and 11, New Horizons, Dawn, NEAR Shoemaker and Kepler.
  • Telling the story: 14 illustrated storybooks, one for each of the 13 groups on NASA's resource list plus Voyager 1, each told by the machine in its own voice.
  • For school-age space fans: short sentences, every big word explained, read-aloud with word-by-word highlighting, a guided journey and two games.
  • The science it made possible: each machine's page links one part (a drill, a seismometer, a radio) to one discovery, and three full mission files add timelines, NASA 3D models and photos.

What we built

  • Guided journey: a short team film, then an astronaut guide who leads visitors from the solar system to Mars, Viking 1's storybook and its mission file.
  • 3D solar system: the planets orbit the Sun; visitors zoom, turn, search for planets and probes, and open each planet's NASA Science page.
  • 3D Moon and Mars globes: tap any machine at its real landing or impact site, filter by status and year, and follow the golden lights that mark machines with a storybook.
  • 14 storybooks: Eagle, Viking 1, Voyager 1, Surveyor, Three Moon Buggies, The Listening Stations (ALSEP), Sojourner, Spirit & Opportunity, Phoenix & InSight, Ingenuity, NEAR Shoemaker, Dawn, Kepler, and Pioneer 10 & 11. Each is read aloud with word highlighting, speed control, music and chapters, and every page names its sources.
  • 3 mission files: Eagle, Viking 1 and Voyager 1, each with a timeline, a NASA 3D model with numbered parts, the landing site, NASA photos and videos, and our own film for Eagle and Viking 1.
  • Field notes: one page for every other machine, with its story, why it was sent, what it discovered, how its hardware worked, where it is now, a NASA photo and sources.
  • Cosmic Library: all 37 machines on one timeline, with search and filters by world and by status (still awake, asleep, planned crash, adrift).
  • Play: Signal Hunter, where players send radio pings to find a lost lander on the Moon or Mars, and Who am I?, where they guess a machine from its riddle.
  • Live Voyager 1 distance: an estimate of how far Voyager 1 is right now, with a countdown to 18 November 2026, when it will be one light-day from Earth.
  • Team films: an opening film, and animations of Apollo 11's and Viking 1's whole journeys.
  • About page: how to explore, how the facts were checked, every citation, accessibility, ideas for teachers and our contact address.
  • Accessibility: a highly legible typeface, full keyboard use, text descriptions for pictures, reduced motion on request, and no accounts or adverts.

How it works

  • A website for any device: a React app that runs in any modern browser on phones, tablets and computers, with nothing to install; each page loads only when it is opened.
  • One catalog of 37 machines: every machine has its NSSDCA record number, world, status, year, coordinates and story in one place, and the globes, Cosmic Library, games and side panels all read from it.
  • Machines in their real places: the latitude and longitude from NASA's records are turned into a point on the 3D Moon or Mars, built with three.js and React Three Fiber.
  • The solar system: planet orbits and periods come from NSSDCA's Planetary Fact Sheets; distances are shortened so every planet fits on screen, and a link to NASA's Eyes on the Solar System gives the true scale.
  • Storybooks: each book is a data file of pages (story text, a "Did you know?" fact, a NASA photo and a source list) plus pictures drawn in code.
  • Read-aloud: Eagle, Viking 1 and Voyager 1 use recorded narration with a time for every word; the other 11 books use the browser's own speech voice, which reports each word as it is spoken, so that word lights up.
  • Live NASA photos: photos load straight from NASA's servers by their NASA number, and the mission files search the NASA Image and Video Library for more; if NASA's servers cannot be reached, a drawn portrait takes the photo's place.
  • Live Voyager 1 distance: calculated from NASA's published one-light-day date and Voyager 1's speed of about 17 km per second.
  • Archive server: a Node.js and Express API with a MySQL database that stores machines, missions, media and sources.

How we made sure the facts are right

  • NASA first: dates, places and numbers come from NASA Science mission pages, NSSDCA records, JPL, NASA History and the NASA Photojournal.
  • A source beside every fact: each storybook page lists its sources, each book lists all of them in its chapters, and every field-notes page and mission file ends with its sources. The About page collects every citation in one place.
  • Careful words: where reliable sources give different numbers, the text says "about" or "more than" instead of picking one.
  • Imagined and real, kept apart: the machines' feelings are a storyteller's device, but every event in the stories really happened.
  • Up to date: facts were checked in November 2026, including Perseverance passing Opportunity's driving record on 11 October 2026 and Voyager 1 switching off another instrument in April 2026.
  • Mistakes fixed in the open: checking found errors in the original data, such as Opportunity drawn about 11° east of its landing site and Lunar Prospector placed on the wrong side of the Moon's south pole. Both are fixed and listed on the About page.

Benefits and intended impact

We want a child to look at the Moon or Mars and know that real machines are resting there, and what each one taught us.

  • From "space junk" to space heritage: children meet the hardware as explorers that finished their work, not as rubbish.
  • Engineering and science as one story: every machine shows how one part made one discovery possible; Viking's arm let it dig for signs of life, and Earth could follow Pioneer 10 past Jupiter because it could still hear its radio.
  • A habit of checking sources: every fact names its source, so readers learn early where knowledge comes from.
  • Free learning for any classroom or home: no account, no installation, and ready activities for teachers on the About page.
  • Reading support: read-aloud with word highlighting, adjustable speed and a highly legible typeface help early and struggling readers.
  • Curiosity about the next missions: knowing what Apollo, Viking and Voyager achieved prepares young readers to follow NASA's next steps to the Moon, Mars and beyond.

Who it is for

  • Children aged about 9 to 15: the main readers; one clear idea per page.
  • Younger or struggling readers, with an adult: read-aloud and word highlighting let them follow along.
  • Teachers and families: ready classroom activities and a source behind every fact.
  • Curious adults and museum or library visitors: mission files and field notes go deeper, with NASA records, photos and 3D models.

What makes it creative

The central idea is that these machines are not dead or abandoned: they are sleeping beauties, each with a story.

  • Machines with a voice: every storybook is a bedtime story told by the machine itself, with friendly faces drawn on the hardware.
  • Status as a feeling: each machine is "still awake", "asleep", "adrift" or ended in a "planned crash", words a child understands at once.
  • A journey, not a list: visitors fly from the whole solar system down to the exact spot where a lander rests, and golden lights show which machines have a storybook.
  • Made for this project: the pictures are drawn in code, the three lullabies (a music box for the Moon, a kalimba for Mars, bells for deep space) are synthesized from scratch, and the films are our own.
  • Learning through play: Signal Hunter turns finding a silent lander into a game of radio pings, and Who am I? turns facts into riddles.
  • Honest storytelling: the feelings are imagined, but every event is real and carries its source.

What we hope to do next

These are suggestions; keep only the ones the team really plans.

  • Recorded narration for all 14 books: the narration tool is already in the project.
  • More languages, starting with Bangla.
  • The view from orbit: add NASA orbital photos of each landing site, from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter for the Moon and HiRISE for Mars.
  • More machines, such as LCROSS and the GRAIL twins, which ended their missions by hitting the Moon.
  • Classroom worksheets to print, and feedback from teachers and children through team.lostinspace.6@gmail.com.

Tools, languages and software

All libraries are open source; no special hardware is needed.

  • Languages: JavaScript (JSX), HTML, CSS, Python and SQL.
  • Website: React 19, React Router 7, Vite 7 and Zustand.
  • 3D worlds and models: three.js, React Three Fiber, drei, React Three postprocessing and glTF/GLB models.
  • Animation and icons: Framer Motion and Lucide icons.
  • Server and data: Node.js with Express, and MySQL 8.
  • Narration: the Kokoro-82M text-to-speech model (Apache 2.0), run locally with kokoro-onnx, ONNX, NumPy, soundfile and FFmpeg; the browser's Web Speech API for the 11 newer books.
  • Music: three original lullabies synthesized in Python with NumPy and FFmpeg.
  • Typefaces: Jost, Atkinson Hyperlegible Next, Fraunces and Literata (SIL Open Font License).
  • Hosting: Vercel.
